name: Stone quarrying with wedge
kb: Drive wedges into natural fissures to break stone blocks
note: Wedges are inserted along planes of weakness, then tapped in sequence to split stone cleanly. Without this, stone quarrying is random fracture, not construction.

name: Stone saw with abrasive
kb: Frame saw with abrasive sand to cut stone into dressed blocks
note: Stone is harder than tools. Abrasive (usually sand) embedded in the saw does the cutting, not the blade. The saw itself serves as a guide.

name: Gang saw for stone
kb: Multiple parallel blades driven by water power to cut stone simultaneously
note: Parallel saws cut multiple blocks simultaneously from one stone blank. The synchronisation problem: slipping and binding destroy either the work or the machine. Requires heavy bearings and careful clearance.

name: Stone polishing and smoothing
kb: Rubbing stone surfaces with abrasive blocks to achieve smoothness
note: Emery or other hard stone grinds softer stone flat. Requires rhythm and feel. Machine polishing comes much later.

name: Lime mortar
kb: Slaked lime mixed with sand, water and sometimes tallow or blood to bind masonry
note: Lime carbonates slowly in air over years. The binder is the product of a chemical reaction you cannot control, only manage with thickness and porosity.

name: Gypsum plaster finish
kb: Calcined gypsum mixed with water for quick-setting finish plaster
note: Gypsum plaster sets in minutes, unlike lime which takes weeks. The speed forces different working methods and cannot be slowed down.

name: Pozzolana hydraulic concrete
kb: Lime and volcanic ash create a binder that sets underwater
note: Pozzolanic reaction between silica and lime happens slowly and imperceptibly. The concrete is weak for months then becomes very hard. No chemical knowledge, only empirical observation of ash quality and mixing ratio.

name: Terrazzo floor finish
kb: Lime mortar with stone chips and marble dust, polished smooth
note: Aggregate size and porosity must be matched to allow polishing down to stone-wide sheen. Under-fired mortar remains soft and yields to the stone dust. Over-fired mortar tears the chips.

name: Artificial cast stone
kb: Lime mortar cast in wooden moulds to create facing stones
note: Eliminates quarrying and stone shaping work. Moulds are reusable but casting and curing is slower than laying natural stone. Works only where artificial facing can pass as masonry.

name: Post and lintel structure
kb: Vertical posts with horizontal beam spanning between them
note: Beam strength and span are limited by its cross-section. Stone and timber beam bending is the constraint that architects worked around for millennia.

name: True arch in stone
kb: Wedge-shaped stones arranged radially, transmitting load laterally to supports
note: Load flows through the curve to the supports, not down through the span. Each stone is under compression only, never tension. Geometry, not material strength, is the constraint.

name: Groin vault in stone
kb: Two barrel vaults intersected at right angles, creating four curved triangular surfaces
note: Two arches cross at right angles. The groin curves are the geometry problem. Vault is self-supporting once completed but extremely delicate during construction.

name: Ribbed vault in stone
kb: Arched stone ribs bear the load, with lighter web filling in between
note: Heavy ribs carry load. Web is incidental, can be thin or even omitted. Ribs can be built first as temporary trusses, supporting the web. Load path becomes clear and traceable.

name: Flying buttress in stone
kb: External arched support transferring vault load outboard to distant pier
note: Takes vault thrust outboard without disrupting interior space. Enables tall nave walls unsupported from inside. The arch does not pass through the wall, it connects at one point.

name: Timber roof truss
kb: Triangulated timber frame with tension ties and compression struts
note: Wood is weak in tension. Truss geometry converts bending into pure tension and compression. Ties must not slip, so joints are critical.

name: King post roof truss
kb: Single vertical post from apex to tie beam, supporting ridge under tension
note: Central post is in compression. Ties spread the apex, pulling down on beam ends. Very old form, but only works for narrow spans.

name: Queen post roof truss
kb: Two posts set back from apex, with central strut and spreading collar tie
note: Two posts working inward reduce the tie-beam span compared to king post, enabling longer roof slopes. Geometry is trickier to lay out.

name: Lattice truss for beams
kb: Timber ribs in criss-cross pattern to create deep beam with minimal weight
note: Removes weight from the centre while keeping depth. Works if all diagonals are tied properly. Joint failures are catastrophic and not obvious until collapse.

name: Warren truss
kb: Diagonal members at 45 degrees with no vertical struts, all triangles pointing same way
note: 45-degree angles mean each member carries load efficiently in pure tension or compression. No shear in diagonals, no verticals needed. Requires precise geometry.

name: Pratt truss
kb: Diagonals slope inward from panel ends, verticals carry shear
note: Diagonals in tension, verticals in compression. Longer diagonals mean shorter verticals. Compression members must not buckle, so they must be heavy or braced.

name: Trussed arch
kb: Arch ribs braced by interior timber trusses to prevent spreading
note: Arch wants to spread. Timber bracing, if properly located and strong, resists the spreading force. Requires coordination of load paths between materials.

name: Space frame three-dimensional truss
kb: Pyramidal cells of tetrahedral trusses creating deep beam in three dimensions
note: Stiffness comes from three-dimensional triangulation, not from depth. Very light for span, but joints are complex and must carry loads in many directions. Assembly is intricate.

name: Cast iron column
kb: Hollow cast iron shaft for vertical load bearing
note: Iron is much stronger than timber in compression. Hollow section is economical. Cast iron is brittle; sudden shock loads can snap columns.

name: Cast iron beam
kb: I-shaped or hollow-section beam cast in one piece
note: Cast iron is much weaker in tension than compression. Bottom fibre is under tension in bending. Beams crack unpredictably. Wrought iron or steel is superior but slower to install.

name: Wrought iron plate girder
kb: Flat plates riveted together to form deep I-shaped beam
note: Riveted plate girders are flexible, not stiff. Many rivets must hold against vibration and stress concentration at holes. Riveting skill is critical.

name: Rolled iron or steel I beam
kb: I-shaped section hot rolled from solid billet in one pass
note: Heating steel to rolling temperature is energy-intensive. Section must be designed to flow evenly through rolls. Dies wear quickly. Economy comes from not riveting.

name: Steel plate girder assembly
kb: Steel plates and angles welded or riveted into deep box girder
note: Stiffness comes from geometric depth, not just material. Web must be braced to prevent buckling. Flanges carry bending, web carries shear.

name: Riveted bolted connection
kb: Hot rivets upset through overlapping plates to create permanent joint
note: Hot rivet is upset under the hammer, growing to fill the hole. Force comes from thermal contraction after cooling. Each rivet must be hand-hammered; no way to speed it up.

name: Bolted connection with nut
kb: Threaded bolt through plates, tightened with wrench and nut
note: Bolt threads must be accurate and consistent. Tightness is limited by thread strength and tool torque. Joints can loosen under vibration unless locked.

name: Electric arc welded joint
kb: Electric arc melts base steel and electrode, creating homogeneous joint
note: Weld is as strong as or stronger than base steel if cooled slowly. Rapid cooling creates brittle martensite. Technique matters enormously: speed, angle, heat input all affect final strength.

name: Gusset plate reinforcement
kb: Diagonal or triangular plates added at joints to carry shear
note: Riveted joints are weak under shear. Gusset plates redirect force along stiffer paths. Excessive riveting in gussets causes stress concentration.

name: Steel frame skeleton building
kb: Multi-storey frame of rolled columns and beams, with non-structural walls
note: Load flows down the steel grid, not through walls. Walls need not be structural, only weathertight. Foundations must carry all load through frame, not spread it.

name: Curtain wall non-structural facade
kb: Lightweight panel hung from floor slab, carrying no structural load
note: Panels are supported only at top, not at sills. Wind load is transmitted through fasteners to the frame. Sealing is critical; no redundancy if one panel fails.

name: Cantilever beam or slab
kb: Beam fixed at one end, projecting unsupported
note: Fixed end experiences very high moment. Deflection is cubic in length, so small overhang looks fine but is actually close to failure.

name: Suspension bridge system
kb: Flexible cable hung from towers suspends deck via vertical hangers
note: Main cable carries all load in tension. Hangers support deck from cable, like a string pulled upward at midspan. Towers must resist enormous horizontal thrust.

name: Steel wire rope and spinning
kb: Twisted steel wires bundled into large-diameter rope under tension
note: Twisting individual wires increases axial stiffness. Rotation of the bundle during spinning must be controlled, otherwise the rope twists itself apart.

name: Cable anchorage block
kb: Massive concrete or steel block anchoring cable at tension, preventing pull-out
note: Cable is wedged and stressed into the block. Cone of stress must stay within mass. If block is too small, wedge pulls free, catapulting cable.

name: Stiffening truss for deck
kb: Deep truss runs along deck, resisting wind and dynamic loads
note: Light decks oscillate in wind. Stiffening truss adds weight and damping. Tuned mass dampers do the same job with less weight, but are harder to design.

name: Box girder or tubular section
kb: Closed hollow section with four sides, resisting torsion effectively
note: Box resists torsion in proportion to enclosed area. Open section (I beam) has no torsional stiffness. Welding the box closed is expensive but essential.

name: Steel arch bridge
kb: Two-hinged or fixed arch of steel, carrying load in compression to abutments
note: Arch must be hinged or buckling becomes a problem. Fixed arch is indeterminate; temperature change and settlement cause internal stress, not reactions.

name: Bascule drawbridge
kb: Counterweighted leaf pivoting up on hinge to allow ship passage
note: Counterweight must balance leaf exactly. Load moves as bridge opens, changing balance. Seals and guides must not jam under any circumstance.

name: Swing bridge on central pivot
kb: Bridge rotates on central post, aligning with river or opening for traffic
note: Pivot must be perfectly centred and smooth. Friction from bridge weight is enormous. Rail must guide bridge smoothly without binding on approach.

name: Pontoon floating bridge
kb: Floating barges or floats lashed together, connected by chains, with deck on top
note: Bridge sinks and rises with water level. Approach ramps must adjust. Pontoons can be removed in winter or when passage is needed.

name: Masonry aqueduct arch bridge
kb: Series of tall arches carrying water channel across valley
note: Water pressure is constant, not dynamic. Channel must be nearly level to maintain flow. Multiple arches share the load; failure of one makes the bridge catastrophically unstable.

name: Inverted siphon pipe
kb: Pipe drops below required level then rises, allowing water to cross obstacles
note: Siphon works by gravity and atmospheric pressure. Air locks destroy the flow. Pipe must be primed and remain full. Sediment accumulates at the low point.

name: Pile driving by drop hammer
kb: Heavy weight dropped onto pile to drive it into soft ground
note: Weight and drop height determine driving force. Pile compresses ground, packing it. As ground gets denser, driving becomes harder; each drop achieves less penetration.

name: Screw pile with helical blade
kb: Spiral blade on shaft screws into ground like a corkscrew
note: Eliminates the hammer and drop. Helix must have correct pitch and angle or pile spins in place without driving. Torque must be balanced; twisted piles lose capacity.

name: Sheet piling wall
kb: Interlocked steel or timber sheets driven side by side to create waterproof wall
note: Interlock must be tight or water seeps between sheets. Each new sheet is pushed down by the ones already driven; last sheets are hardest to drive.

name: Caisson cofferdam box
kb: Watertight box sunk to bedrock, filled with air, allowing work underwater
note: Box is heavy, sinks under its own weight. Must be sealed at corners and joints. Explosive decompression if air is lost. Caisson disease kills workers who decompress too fast.

name: Pneumatic caisson with air pressure
kb: Compressed air pumped into caisson keeps water out at depth
note: Air pressure must equal water pressure at working depth. Divers descend and work in high pressure. Sand boils unexpectedly when pressure drops, sucking water under walls.

name: Cofferdam temporary barrier
kb: Temporary enclosure of sheet pile or timber, pumped dry for work
note: Simple dike around the work area, then pump it empty. Leakage increases as water pressure builds. Backup pump must run continuously.

name: Diaphragm wall with slurry
kb: Slurry-filled trench with concrete wall cast in place
note: Bentonite slurry supports trench walls without temporary shoring. Concrete is heavier than slurry, so it sinks and replaces it. Requires careful placement and tremie.

name: Underpinning of existing structure
kb: Installing new foundation beneath existing building without damage
note: Building must be supported while old foundation is removed and new one installed. Settlement of even 1mm can crack walls. Shoring must be adjustable and carefully monitored.

name: Dewatering system with pumps
kb: Pumps remove groundwater from foundation excavation
note: Lowering water table causes settlement of nearby buildings. Particles clog pumps and seals. Two pumps must run simultaneously; if one fails, site floods in minutes.

name: Soil compaction by roller
kb: Heavy roller or rammer compacts soil in lifts, increasing bearing capacity
note: Soil density increases with each pass, but benefit decreases. Optimal moisture content exists; too wet or too dry, soil resists compaction.

name: Retaining wall gravity structure
kb: Massive masonry wall holding back soil pressure
note: Wall must be heavy enough that soil pressure cannot overturn it. Base angle and drainage affect stability. Passive pressure of soil in front of toe adds resistance.

name: Gravity dam masonry structure
kb: Massive triangular dam wall where weight resists water pressure
note: Must not slide on foundation. Foundation must be rock; soil underneath cannot support the load. Uplift pressure under base can lift dam like a balloon.

name: Arch dam curved structure
kb: Curved arch carries water load horizontally to valley walls
note: Arch curve reduces mass needed compared to gravity dam. Abutments must be strong and rock; bad foundations cause catastrophic failure.

name: Earth dam with clay core
kb: Compacted earth with impermeable clay core, gravel and filter zones
note: Core must be more impermeable than surrounding zones or seepage concentrates. Piping failure (internal erosion) is sudden and catastrophic. Requires continuous monitoring.

name: Spillway overflow structure
kb: Controlled overflow channel protecting dam from overtopping
note: High-velocity water in spillway can erode concrete. Stilling basin dissipates energy. Spillway must never be overtopped; if crest elevation is wrong, whole dam fails.

name: Tunnel by cut and cover
kb: Open trench with roof beam and arch or vault cover, then backfill
note: Roof must support all overburden load plus live load above. Shallow tunnels this way. Deep tunnels need shield method.

name: Tunnel shield method
kb: Steel cylinder pushed forward, excavating at front, lining installed behind
note: Shield is pushed forward by jacks. Face is pressurised or shielded to prevent collapse. Rings are bolted together as shield advances. Grout fills void behind.

name: Drill and blast tunnel
kb: Holes drilled in rock face, filled with explosives, detonated in sequence
note: Blast timing is critical. Wrong sequence creates large boulders and poor fragmentation. Too much explosive wastes powder and damages rock walls.

name: Tunnel permanent lining
kb: Cast concrete rings bolted together inside tunnel to support walls
note: Segments are cast and cured before installation. Installation is quick, 1-2 rings per day. Joints must be tight; water ingress rots concrete.

name: Ventilation shaft and duct
kb: Secondary shaft for air circulation in long tunnels
note: Shaft is usually shallower than main tunnel. Ventilation depends on natural stack effect or mechanical fans. Pressure difference drives flow.

name: Treadwheel crane
kb: Large wooden wheel driven by workers walking inside it
note: Mechanical advantage comes from wheel radius. Internal braking is essential; if rope breaks, load and cage slam down, killing occupants.

name: Derrick crane with guy lines
kb: Tall mast held by cables and guy ropes, hook suspended from peak
note: Stays on the mast must be tight or it whips in wind. Mast is weak against side load. Guy cables must be tensioned equally or mast bends.

name: Tower crane on fixed base
kb: Steel tower with rotating jib and hoist, electrically driven
note: Jib and load are cantilevered. Base must be heavy to resist overturning moment. Wind creates side load; bracing must hold or tower tilts.

name: Block and tackle with rope
kb: Fixed and movable pulleys multiply force by rope arrangement
note: Mechanical advantage equals number of rope parts under load. Rope must not slip on sheaves. Friction in blocks reduces actual advantage by 10-20 percent.

name: Timber scaffolding system
kb: Temporary timber framework lashed together with rope and planks for worker access
note: Lashing discipline is critical. A single untied rope can unravel the whole frame. Deflection under load is visible and causes worker fear.

name: Elevator with safety brake
kb: Counterweighted cage with mechanical brake that grips guide rails if rope breaks
note: Brake works only if jaws are pre-tensioned by cable tension. As rope breaks, tension drops, triggering brake. Wedge angle must be perfect or brake slips.

name: Plumbing vertical stack system
kb: Lead or iron pipe stacks for water supply and waste drainage
note: Waste must slope correctly or it backs up. Soil pipe must be large to prevent siphoning. Supply lines must be sloped so air cannot trap high points.

name: Trap with water seal
kb: U-bend under sink that holds water to block sewer gas and pests
note: Water seal is only 5-10cm. Siphoning or evaporation breaks it. Every fixture must have a trap or smell is unbearable.

name: Sewer gravity drainage network
kb: Underground pipes collecting and transporting waste to treatment or discharge
note: Network effect: one house benefits little; system must serve whole city. Slopes must be precise or sediment settles. Cleanouts must be spaced to allow maintenance.

name: Water main distribution pipe
kb: Underground pipeline supplying water to district
note: Pipe must be buried below frost line or it freezes. Corrosion creates holes; no way to inspect or repair without excavation. Pressure rating must be adequate.

name: Damp proof course barrier layer
kb: Impermeable layer in wall preventing capillary rise of moisture
note: Capillary rise can be metres high in masonry. Moisture triggers rot and salt crystallisation. Damp proof course breaks the capillary chain.

name: Cavity wall with air space
kb: Two separate leaves of masonry with air gap, stopping moisture penetration
note: Outer leaf weathers, inner leaf stays dry. Ties hold leaves together but create thermal bridges. Cavity must be kept clean or moisture settles.

name: Central heating hot water system
kb: Boiler heats water circulated through pipes to radiators
note: Boiler must be kept filled and bleed of air. Expansion tank absorbs water expanding as it heats. Radiators must drain when not in use or freeze.

name: Cast iron radiator
kb: Cast iron section carrying hot water, radiating heat to room
note: Fins increase surface area for heat transfer. Scaling inside radiators reduces heat flow; circulation must be clean. Thermostat valve controls flow independently.

name: Forced ventilation mechanical system
kb: Fan driven by motor or steam engine pushes air through ducts
note: Ducting must be sized to prevent noise and vibration. Fan noise increases as speed increases. Dampers must adjust flow without complete closure or stall.

name: Fire escape stairs and landings
kb: External metal stairway providing emergency exit route
note: Stairs must not be obstructed or lockable. Pivot hinge ladder can trap people if hinge seizes. Many fire escape deaths were from mechanism failure, not fire.

name: Automatic fire sprinkler
kb: Heat-triggered valve on water pipe, spraying room when temperature rises
note: Thermal element must melt reliably at set temperature. Solder plug can fail if handled. Water pressure must be adequate to drive flow at all nozzles.

name: Plate glass large pane
kb: Polished sheet glass cast and ground flat, large transparent panes
note: Casting is slow and expensive. Annealing must be carefully controlled or internal stress cracks glass months later. Each large pane is handmade and unique.

name: Sash window with cord and weight
kb: Two glass panes slide vertically in wooden frame, balanced by counterweights
note: Cord wears and breaks; rope must be threaded through pulleys. Weights must exactly balance panes or window stays open or slams shut.

name: Roof truss with corrugated iron
kb: Wooden or steel truss supporting corrugated sheet metal roof
note: Corrugations are structural; corrugated iron is much stiffer than flat. Fastening through corrugations creates stress concentration. Expansion and contraction create noise.

name: Asphalt roll roofing and shingles
kb: Bitumen-impregnated felt, laid in overlapping layers with hot tar
note: Installation temperature is critical. Too cold, bitumen cracks; too hot, it flows away. Laps must overlap correctly to shed water downslope, not trap it.

name: Building insulation materials
kb: Fibrous or cellular materials filling cavities and reducing heat transfer
note: Insulation works by trapping air in cells. Compression destroys it. Vapour barrier is needed or condensation saturates insulation in cold climates.

name: Rotary concrete mixer drum
kb: Rotating drum tumbles concrete ingredients to uniform mix
note: Drum must rotate at optimum speed. Too slow, materials segregate; too fast, centrifugal force throws concrete outward. Discharge gate must not jam with set material.

name: Vibratory compaction of concrete
kb: Electric or pneumatic vibrators eliminate air pockets in fresh concrete
note: Over-vibration segregates aggregate from paste. Under-vibration leaves voids and weak zones. Duration is only 5-10 seconds per area.

name: Formwork and shuttering system
kb: Temporary wooden or steel mould supporting concrete until cured
note: Formwork must be strong enough to hold wet concrete without deflection. Deflection continues after striking, permanently distorting the concrete surface.

name: Slipform creeping formwork
kb: Formwork slowly rises as concrete cures, allowing continuous pour
note: Creep rate must be controlled so concrete sets enough to hold form weight. Too fast, concrete breaks; too slow, set concrete cracks from form friction.

name: Sprayed concrete shotcrete
kb: Concrete sprayed at high velocity onto surface, compacted in flight
note: Rebound of aggregate on vertical surfaces wastes material. Air pressure and nozzle angle control placement. Curing must be slow to prevent drying shrinkage cracks.

name: Expansion joint control system
kb: Gaps and filler materials allowing concrete movement from temperature change
note: Concrete expands 10-15 mm per 100 metres with 50 degree temperature change. Filler must compress, not extrude. Spacing closer than 20 metres is normal.

name: Reinforced concrete slab and beam
kb: Steel bars in tension zones of concrete element counteract concrete cracking
note: Steel and concrete have nearly identical thermal expansion; if not, the bond breaks every summer and they separate. This accidental match made reinforced concrete possible.

name: Deformed reinforcing bar
kb: Steel rod with ribs or deformations for better concrete bond
note: Ribs cut into the surface create mechanical bond better than friction. Bond failure is difficult to detect until beam collapses. Testing requires destructive sampling.

name: Prestressed concrete element
kb: Steel cables stressed before concrete sets, then released, creating internal compression
note: Stressing imparts compression that cancels tensile stress from bending. Longer spans and thinner sections are possible. Stress loss over time requires careful design margins.

name: Post tensioning with stressing jacks
kb: Cables stressed after concrete hardens using large hydraulic jacks
note: Jacks apply huge force; hydraulic failure kills workers. Ducts for cables must be placed accurately or stressing is uneven, causing internal damage.

name: Precast concrete panel
kb: Concrete element cast off-site in controlled conditions, transported and erected
note: Factory control improves quality and speed. Transport is expensive; distance limits economy. Connections between panels are weak points; connection design is critical.

name: Portland cement powder
kb: Calcined limestone and clay ground to powder, hydrates with water
note: Clinkering temperature is 1450 C. Clinker is the active phase; grinding it fine increases early strength but consumes energy. Raw materials must be fed as slurry.

name: Rotary cement kiln
kb: Large rotating drum maintaining clinkering temperature for continuous production
note: Kiln rotates 1-3 rpm. Material must not stick to walls or discharge will jam. Flame temperature at inlet must reach 1800 C. Insulation must survive 1450 C inside.

name: Cement clinker mill grinding
kb: Ball mill or roller mill grinds clinker to fine powder for cement
note: Grinding heats cement. If overheated, early hydration begins in the mill, weakening final product. Cooling is essential. Ball mill creates abrasive dust that wears liners.
